beats.title: The Audio Delay Problem
beats.body: Every time a sound played in GDevelop, a brand-new audio instance was created on demand, causing a perceptible delay before playback. The PR proposes caching audio instances so they can be reused and optionally preloaded during the game's loading screen, eliminating that latency.

beats.title: API Design: Fluent Chaining vs. Explicit Getters/Setters
beats.body: The contributor added method chaining (fluent interface) to the audio wrapper class to mirror the style of the underlying audio library. The project owner questioned whether this convenience was worth the cost: fluent methods resist static typing, may hinder runtime optimization, and obscure intent compared to explicit getter/setter pairs.

beats.title: Position A — arthuro555
beats.body: Fluent chaining mirrors the external library's own API, giving JavaScript developers a familiar and consistent experience. However, arthuro555 also flagged that replacing the old overloaded methods with the new getter/setter style is a breaking change for any game developer using JavaScript events directly.
beats.author: arthuro555

beats.title: Position B — 4ian
beats.body: Explicit getters and setters are not verbose and are far clearer for static analysis and JIT compilation. The owner also argued that exposing the audio wrapper as a fully public API risks memory leaks if users create instances outside the managed sound system, suggesting it should remain an internal implementation detail.
beats.author: 4ian

beats.question: Given the tradeoffs between API familiarity, static-typing safety, and backward compatibility, what API design would you choose for the audio wrapper and why?
